Summary: This EAACI position paper provides a comprehensive review and management recommendations for ocular allergy, covering seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis, vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, and contact blepharoconjunctivitis. It evaluates evidence for topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and allergen immunotherapy. The aim is to guide specialists in the treatment of these conditions.

Conditions covered:
  - Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
  - Perennial allergic conjunctivitis
  - Vernal keratoconjunctivitis
  - Atopic keratoconjunctivitis
  - Contact blepharoconjunctivitis

Target population:
  - Patients with ocular allergy
  - Adults
  - Children

Therapeutic areas:
  - Topical antihistamines
  - Mast cell stabilizers
  - Dual-acting agents
  - Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
  - Corticosteroids
  - Calcineurin inhibitors
  - Allergen-specific immunotherapy
  - Biologics
  - Non-pharmacological interventions

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Seasonal Allergic Conjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - SAC
  Description: Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity disorder of the conjunctiva triggered by seasonal airborne allergens, such as pollens.
  Clinical presentation: Ocular itching, redness, tearing, and swelling that occur during specific seasons coinciding with allergen exposure.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history and symptom assessment
      Purpose: Identify seasonal pattern and potential triggers.
      When indicated: Always
    - Test: In vivo allergen tests (e.g., skin prick test)
      Purpose: Confirm IgE sensitization to seasonal allergens.
      When indicated: When specific allergen identification is required.
    - Test: In vitro specific IgE measurement
      Purpose: Detect allergen-specific IgE antibodies in serum.
      When indicated: When skin testing is unavailable or contraindicated.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_02
  Name: Perennial Allergic Conjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - PAC
  Description: Perennial allergic conjunctivitis is an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity disorder of the conjunctiva triggered by year-round allergens, such as house dust mites, animal dander, or molds.
  Clinical presentation: Chronic ocular itching, redness, tearing, and swelling with perennial, often fluctuating, symptoms.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history and symptom assessment
      Purpose: Identify perennial pattern and potential indoor triggers.
      When indicated: Always
    - Test: In vivo allergen tests (e.g., skin prick test)
      Purpose: Confirm IgE sensitization to perennial allergens.
      When indicated: When specific allergen identification is required.
    - Test: In vitro specific IgE measurement
      Purpose: Detect allergen-specific IgE antibodies in serum.
      When indicated: When skin testing is unavailable or contraindicated.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_03
  Name: Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - VKC
  Description: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a persistent, chronic ocular allergic disorder with both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated mechanisms, often occurring in children and characterized by severe inflammation and potential corneal complications.
  Clinical presentation: Severe ocular itching, photophobia, tearing, mucous discharge, giant papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, and possible corneal involvement such as shield ulcers.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Ophthalmic examination
      Purpose: Assess conjunctival and corneal involvement (giant papillae, limbal infiltrates, corneal erosions).
      When indicated: Suspected VKC
    - Test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE)
      Purpose: Identify contributing allergens, although VKC may not be solely IgE-driven.
      When indicated: When allergic triggers are suspected.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_04
  Name: Atopic Keratoconjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - AKC
  Description: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a severe, sight-threatening chronic allergic eye disease associated with atopic dermatitis, involving both IgE- and non-IgE-mediated pathways.
  Clinical presentation: Eyelid eczema, intense itching, conjunctival inflammation, corneal damage, and potential visual impairment. Often associated with systemic atopy.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Ophthalmic examination
      Purpose: Evaluate eyelid, conjunctival, and corneal involvement.
      When indicated: Suspected AKC
    - Test: Allergy testing (skin prick or serum IgE)
      Purpose: Identify possible allergic triggers.
      When indicated: When allergic components are present.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_05
  Name: Contact Blepharoconjunctivitis
  Synonyms:
    - CBC
  Description: Contact blepharoconjunctivitis is a non-IgE-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction of the eyelids and conjunctiva caused by contact with allergens, such as cosmetics, topical medications, or environmental agents.
  Clinical presentation: Eyelid eczema, itching, inflammation, and conjunctival involvement, often after exposure to a specific topical agent.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Patch testing
      Purpose: Identify the causative contact allergen.
      When indicated: When CBC is suspected.
    - Test: Ophthalmic and dermatologic examination
      Purpose: Assess eyelid and conjunctival changes.
      When indicated: Always

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Start therapy with topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-acting agents, as they are all effective in reducing signs and symptoms.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-acting agents
      Evidence level: high
      Recommendation grade: strong
      Summary: These agents are effective in reducing signs and symptoms of SAC. Dual-acting agents may provide quicker symptom relief and may be preferred. Specific agents include olopatadine, ketotifen, epinastine, and alcaftadine (only available in the US).
      Key outcomes: Improvement in ocular symptom scores compared to placebo; no significant differences between individual agents in most studies; alcaftadine may offer superior itch relief.
      Duration cycles: Throughout the allergy season, as needed.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: systemic antihistamines
      Evidence level: moderate
      Summary: Oral antihistamines may be used when ocular symptoms are associated with other allergic comorbidities, such as rhinitis.
      Conditions for use: Concomitant allergic rhinitis or other systemic allergy symptoms.
    - Name: intranasal corticosteroids
      Evidence level: high
      Summary: Effective for ocular symptoms associated with allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, but should be reserved for patients with nasal symptoms.
      Conditions for use: Only if rhinitis is also present; not recommended for isolated ocular symptoms.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids
      Reason: Rarely needed in SAC; should be reserved for acute exacerbations or corneal involvement and used with caution.
    - Name: leukotriene inhibitors
      Reason: Less efficacious than oral antihistamines in adult SAC patients.
    - Name: topical vasoconstrictors
      Reason: Only alleviate hyperemia; risk of tachyphylaxis and side effects with prolonged use; limit to 5-7 days.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of specific and non-specific triggers.
    - Cold compresses, good eyelid hygiene, and lubricants.
    - Preservative-free formulations should be used when possible to minimize ocular surface toxicity.
  Special considerations: Frequent application throughout the day is recommended during the allergy season. Alcaftadine is not available in the EU.

  Condition ref: cond_02
  Setting: first_line

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_03
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: SAC patients with acute exacerbations, corneal involvement, or insufficient response to first-line therapy
  Decision rules:
    - If symptoms are not controlled with topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers or if corneal involvement occurs, consider adding a short course of topical corticosteroids under ophthalmologist supervision.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (short course)
      Summary: Used as short, pulsed therapy for acute exacerbations or corneal involvement, with close monitoring for side effects.
      Key outcomes: Rapid control of inflammation, but risk of increased intraocular pressure, cataract, and infection.
      Duration cycles: Short course; duration should be minimized.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical cyclosporine A 0.1%
      Summary: On-label in EU; used as a steroid-sparing agent in steroid-dependent patients, in specialized centers.
      Conditions for use: Steroid-dependent cases or when frequent corticosteroid use is required.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: tacrolimus 0.1% eye drops
      Reason: Reserved for severe VKC and AKC refractory to cyclosporine; off-label in EU for SAC/PAC.
  Supportive care:
    - Ophthalmologist monitoring for intraocular pressure and cataract formation during corticosteroid use.
  Special considerations: Corticosteroids should not be used as first-line in SAC due to safety concerns. They are reserved for severe or complicated cases.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_05
  Condition ref: cond_03
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with vernal keratoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Initial management includes general measures and symptomatic treatment. Topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers may be tried, but are often insufficient alone. Oral antihistamines can be used for itching, and topical corticosteroids for acute exacerbations.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: oral antihistamines
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Used to alleviate eyelid itching and inflammation.
      Duration cycles: As needed.
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Applied as ointments or creams for acute phases of eyelid eczema; low potency agents such as hydrocortisone, desonide, triamcinolone acetonide are preferred.
      Duration cycles: Short courses during flares.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-acting agents
      Evidence level: moderate
      Summary: A systematic review of 20 RCTs showed improvement in ocular symptoms with these agents, but no specific agent is recommended over another.
      Conditions for use: May be considered as initial therapy, but often insufficient for severe VKC.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of irritants and allergens.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
    - Cold compresses and lubricants.
  Special considerations: VKC is a severe chronic condition; early specialist referral is advised.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_06
  Condition ref: cond_04
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Initial management focuses on eyelid eczema and surface disease. Avoid triggers, maintain lid hygiene, use emollients. Oral antihistamines can be used for itching, and topical corticosteroids for acute flares.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: oral antihistamines
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Used to alleviate eyelid itching.
      Duration cycles: As needed.
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Ointments or creams for acute eyelid eczema; low potency agents preferred.
      Duration cycles: Short courses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical calcineurin inhibitors (skin ointment 0.03% or 0.1%)
      Evidence level: low
      Summary: Useful for lid eczema in AKC; burning sensation is common and secondary infections have been reported.
      Conditions for use: When corticosteroids are insufficient or to reduce steroid exposure.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: topical antihistamines/mast cell stabilizers
      Reason: Evidence for AKC is limited to case reports; not generally recommended.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of irritants/sensitizing antigens.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
  Special considerations: AKC may require systemic immunosuppression in refractory cases with visual threat; cyclosporine is most commonly used, alternatives are tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_07
  Condition ref: cond_03
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: VKC patients with steroid-dependent disease or requiring long-term control
  Decision rules:
    - In patients requiring frequent or prolonged corticosteroids, consider adding topical cyclosporine 0.1% as a steroid-sparing agent.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical cyclosporine A 0.1%
      Summary: On-label in EU; used to reduce steroid dependence in VKC, under specialist supervision.
      Key outcomes: Reduces need for topical corticosteroids.
      Duration cycles: Long-term, as needed.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: tacrolimus 0.1% eye drops
      Summary: Off-label in EU; reserved for severe VKC refractory to cyclosporine.
      Conditions for use: Severe VKC unresponsive to cyclosporine.
  Supportive care:
    - Regular monitoring for ocular surface health, infection, and intraocular pressure.
  Special considerations: Tacrolimus should only be used in specialized centers.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_08
  Condition ref: cond_04
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: AKC patients with steroid-dependent disease or requiring long-term control
  Decision rules:
    - For steroid-dependent AKC, use topical cyclosporine 0.1% as a steroid-sparing agent. If refractory, consider tacrolimus 0.1%. For visual-threatening disease, systemic immunosuppression may be needed.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical cyclosporine A 0.1%
      Summary: On-label in EU; used as steroid-sparing agent in AKC.
      Duration cycles: Long-term.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: tacrolimus 0.1% eye drops
      Summary: Off-label; for AKC refractory to cyclosporine.
      Conditions for use: Refractory AKC.
    - Name: systemic immunosuppression (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil)
      Summary: For refractory AKC with visual threat; cyclosporine is most commonly used.
      Conditions for use: Visual-threatening AKC not controlled with topical agents.
  Supportive care:
    - Ophthalmologist monitoring for drug toxicity.
    - Management of side effects of systemic immunosuppressants.
  Special considerations: Systemic immunosuppression should be prescribed only by specialists.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_09
  Condition ref: cond_05
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with contact blepharoconjunctivitis
  Decision rules:
    - Identify and avoid the offending agent. Use lid hygiene and emollients. For acute eczema, low-potency topical corticosteroids can be applied.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: topical corticosteroids (low potency)
      Summary: For acute phases of eyelid eczema; use low-potency agents such as hydrocortisone, desonide, triamcinolone acetonide.
      Duration cycles: Short courses during flares.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: topical calcineurin inhibitors (skin ointment 0.03% or 0.1%)
      Summary: Useful for lid eczema; tolerability may be limited by burning sensation.
      Conditions for use: When corticosteroids are insufficient or long-term use is needed.
  Supportive care:
    - Avoidance of identified allergens/irritants.
    - Eyelid hygiene.
    - Emollients and skin moisturizing agents.
  Special considerations: Secondary infections may occur with calcineurin inhibitor use, requiring vigilance.

Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_10
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: second_line
  Patient population: Patients with seasonal allergic conjunctivitis with specific IgE sensitization, who have failed or are intolerant to first-line pharmacotherapy, or who wish to modify disease course
  Biomarker condition: Specific IgE sensitization to clinically relevant allergens
  Decision rules:
    - Offer allergen immunotherapy when allergens are clearly identified and symptoms are not adequately controlled with topical agents, or to achieve long-term tolerance.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: allergen-specific immunotherapy (subcutaneous or sublingual)
      Evidence level: high
      Recommendation grade: strong
      Summary: Both SCIT and SLIT are effective in reducing ocular symptom scores and medication use in allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Grass pollen SLIT tablets have shown significant clinical impact.
      Key outcomes: SLIT reduced total ocular symptom score (SMD -0.41 [-0.53;-0.28]), with similar efficacy to SCIT. For grass pollen SLIT tablets, relative clinical impact -29.6% (-23% to -37%) in symptom scores.
      Duration cycles: Typically 3 years or more.
  Supportive care:
    - Management of local and systemic reactions during immunotherapy buildup and maintenance.
    - Patient education on adherence and recognition of adverse events.
  Special considerations: Immunotherapy should be prescribed and supervised by an allergy specialist. For perennial allergens, evidence of symptom reduction is less robust. SLIT is a convenient alternative to SCIT.

  Title: Figure 2. Treatment algorithm for different forms and severities of ocular allergy
  Source heading: 5. Final TF recommendations (Figure 2)
  Description: Algorithm for managing ocular allergy by subtype and severity:

1. Allergic Conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC): Start with avoidance, cold compresses, eyelid hygiene, and lubricants. If symptoms persist, use topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, or dual-action agents (first-line). For moderate/severe cases or comorbid rhinitis, add systemic antihistamines. In acute exacerbations with corneal involvement, consider short-pulsed topical corticosteroids under ophthalmologist supervision. If steroid-dependent, switch to topical calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine, then tacrolimus). Consider allergen immunotherapy if specific sensitization is proven.

2. Vernal/AK Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC/AKC): Begin with avoidance of triggers, eyelid hygiene, and lubricants. For mild cases, start topical antihistamines or mast cell stabilizers. Moderate cases may require short-term topical corticosteroids; severe cases may need pulsed high-dose steroids. For steroid-dependent or severe corneal involvement, initiate topical cyclosporine (0.1% CE if available) or tacrolimus. Refractory cases may need systemic immunosuppression (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, mycophenolate). AIT may be considered on a case-by-case basis.

3. Contact Blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC): Management focuses on allergen avoidance, eyelid hygiene, emollients, and topical low-potency corticosteroids for eczema flares. Topical calcineurin inhibitor ointments can be used for lid eczema.
  Summary: Stepwise therapeutic approach for ocular allergy, differentiating between mild/moderate SAC/PAC, severe VKC/AKC, and CBC, incorporating avoidance, pharmacotherapy, and immunotherapy as appropriate.
  Clinical relevance: Guides clinicians through decision-making based on disease subtype and severity, ensuring appropriate escalation from topical agents to immunomodulators and specialist referral.

Special populations:
  Population: Pregnancy
  Considerations: Few reports on management in pregnant or lactating women. Allergen avoidance and environmental measures are first-line. Mast cell stabilizer eye drops can be used. Topical antihistamines or dual-acting drugs may be tried safely, though many are FDA category C. Short courses of topical corticosteroids are cautiously permitted if needed. Vasoconstrictors and decongestants are generally avoided. Systemic medications should be minimized. Second-generation oral antihistamines can be used (no teratogenic effects reported, low secretion in breast milk). Immunotherapy may be continued but not initiated during pregnancy.
  Treatment modifications: Avoid vasoconstrictors/decongestants. Minimize systemic medications. Prefer second-generation oral antihistamines. Do not initiate immunotherapy; continuation only if already ongoing.

Special populations:
  Population: Children
  Considerations: Topical eye drops approved for adults are generally approved for children over 3 years old. Advise closing the punctum to reduce systemic absorption. First-generation antihistamines are not indicated due to sedative effects; second-generation antihistamines have a good long-term safety profile in pediatrics. Not licensed under 6 months of age.
  Treatment modifications: Close punctum during drop instillation. Avoid first-generation antihistamines. Do not use in infants under 6 months.

Special populations:
  Population: Elderly people
  Considerations: Ocular allergy may persist or appear de novo in the elderly. Age-related structural changes of the eyelid and ocular surface often mimic dry eye disease. Comorbidities and drug interactions limit treatment options. Systemic and local corticosteroids should be limited to short courses due to risks (diabetes, hypertension, osteoporosis, cataract, glaucoma). Topical and systemic decongestants and systemic antihistamines may cause dryness and should be avoided. Cumulative anticholinergic burden from antihistamines and other drugs must be considered.
  Treatment modifications: Limit corticosteroid duration. Avoid decongestants and systemic antihistamines. Assess cumulative anticholinergic effects.
